etymology: Hebrew Emim, terrors or terrible ones, from the root ayom, dreadful. The name is not what they called themselves but what their neighbours called them: the Moabites call them Emims (Deuteronomy 2:11). A whole people known to history only by the fear they produced.
biblical_def: The Emims were the aboriginal inhabitants of the plateau that afterward belonged to Moab, and Scripture describes them in the same breath as the Anakims: a people great, and many, and tall (Deuteronomy 2:10), accounted giants. They appear once in the narrative of Abraham’s day, when Chedorlaomer and the eastern kings swept down the King’s Highway and smote the Rephaims in Ashteroth Karnaim, and the Zuzims in Ham, and the Emims in Shaveh Kiriathaim (Genesis 14:5). After that they are gone, and Moab holds their country. Moses rehearses this to Israel for a particular purpose. As the nation came up the east side of the Dead Sea, God forbade them to touch Moab: Distress not the Moabites, neither contend with them in battle… because I have given Ar unto the children of Lot for a possession (Deuteronomy 2:9). Then, parenthetically, He tells them who used to live there and what became of them. Israel was about to face the Anakims in Canaan and was terrified of them; Moses answers the fear by pointing across the valley and observing that a people just as tall once held that ground, and Lot’s children hold it now, and God arranged the transfer. The giants of Canaan are not an argument against the promise. They are its ordinary raw material.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 has no EMIM entry. The Hebrew name means terrors, and the Authorized Version transliterates it in the plural as Emims, keeping the Hebrew plural ending rather than anglicizing it.
webster_full: EMIMS, n. pl. — Terrible ones; the ancient giant people of the land afterward held by Moab, east of the Dead Sea.
The Hebrew plural -im is retained in the English of the Authorized Version, as with Anakims, Rephaims, Zamzummims, and Zuzims.
The name is descriptive rather than tribal: what their neighbours called them for the terror they inspired (Deuteronomy 2:11).
They are reckoned with the Rephaim, the general Old Testament designation for the tall peoples of the land before Israel.
Webster 1828 does not treat these transliterations; the sense comes wholly from Genesis 14 and Deuteronomy 2.
scriptures: Genesis 14:5
And in the fourteenth year came Chedorlaomer, and the kings that were with him, and smote the Rephaims in Ashteroth Karnaim, and the Zuzims in Ham, and the Emims in Shaveh Kiriathaim,
Deuteronomy 2:9

And the LORD said unto me, Distress not the Moabites, neither contend with them in battle: for I will not give thee of their land for a possession; because I have given Ar unto the children of Lot for a possession.
Deuteronomy 2:10
The Emims dwelt therein in times past, a people great, and many, and tall, as the Anakims;
Deuteronomy 2:11
Which also were accounted giants, as the Anakims; but the Moabites call them Emims.
Acts 17:26
And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Moses’ own use of the Emims: God removes giants routinely, and a believer’s fear of what is large is answered by history, not by flattery.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The recovery here is a method of pastoral encouragement that has almost disappeared. Israel’s fear at Kadeshbarnea was specific: the cities are great and walled up to heaven; and moreover we have seen the sons of the Anakims there. Moses does not answer that fear by telling Israel she is stronger than she thinks. He answers it by recounting what God did to the Emims, the Zamzummims, and the Horims — three peoples every bit as tall, every one of them dispossessed, and none of them by Israel. The encouragement is entirely about God’s ordinary practice, and not at all about Israel’s capacity. Modern exhortation almost always inverts this, and produces a courage that collapses the moment the walls are actually seen.

The second thing to name is the humility of the record. A people great, many, and tall held a fertile plateau for generations and left no monument in Scripture except a name meaning terrors, given them by someone else. Their walls came down, their cities passed to Lot’s children, and the whole account occupies two verses in a parenthesis. Nations do not read their own obituaries. The Christian who takes this seriously will hold his own age’s permanence loosely, and will not be greatly impressed by anything merely large.
roots_summary: Hebrew Emim (H368), terrors, terrible ones, from ayom (H366), dreadful; reckoned among the Rephaim (H7497), the giants.
roots_lines: Hebrew Emim (H368) — the Emims; terrors, from the root for dread.
Hebrew ayom (H366) — terrible, dreadful; used of the beloved in Song of Solomon 6:4 and of the Chaldeans in Habakkuk 1:7.
Hebrew Rephaim (H7497) — the giants; the general class in which Deuteronomy 2:11 reckons the Emims.
Hebrew Anaqim (H6062) — the Anakims; the standard of size against which the Emims are measured.
Hebrew Shaveh Qiryathayim — the plain of Kiriathaim, where Chedorlaomer smote them (Genesis 14:5).
usage: A people great, and many, and tall, as the Anakims (Deuteronomy 2:10) — the measure of what God had already removed.
The Moabites call them Emims (Deuteronomy 2:11) — a nation remembered only by the fear it caused.
Smote… the Emims in Shaveh Kiriathaim (Genesis 14:5) — their single appearance in the narrative.

etymology: Hebrew Zamzummim, commonly explained as murmurers or noisy ones, from a root suggesting a buzzing or unintelligible speech — the sound a foreign giant people made to the ear of the Ammonites who named them. They are generally identified with the Zuzims of Genesis 14:5.
biblical_def: The Zamzummims held the land east of Jordan that afterward belonged to Ammon, and Scripture gives them one parenthesis: That also was accounted a land of giants: giants dwelt therein in old time; and the Ammonites call them Zamzummims; a people great, and many, and tall, as the Anakims; but the LORD destroyed them before them; and they succeeded them, and dwelt in their stead (Deuteronomy 2:20-21). Every clause matters. They were giants; they were numerous; and the agent of their removal is named without ambiguity — the LORD destroyed them, and Ammon merely moved in. This is stated to a nation forbidden to touch Ammon: distress them not, nor meddle with them… because I have given it unto the children of Lot for a possession (Deuteronomy 2:19). Israel is thus told, in the same paragraph, both that she may not take Ammon’s land and why Ammon has it at all. The eastern kings had already struck the same region in Abraham’s day, when Chedorlaomer smote… the Zuzims in Ham. Two names, one people, one end. Og of Bashan, who remained of the remnant of giants, is the last of that stock Israel actually met.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 has no ZAMZUMMIM entry; the word is a Hebrew plural transliterated directly by the King James translators, and its sense is supplied by Deuteronomy 2:20-21 alone.
webster_full: ZAMZUMMIMS, n. pl. — The Ammonite name for the giant people who inhabited the land east of Jordan before them.
The name is usually derived from a root meaning to murmur or hum — the babble of a strange tongue heard from outside.
Genesis 14:5 calls a people of that region the Zuzims; the two names are generally taken of the same stock.
Deuteronomy reckons them with the Rephaim, as it does the Emims and the Anakims.
The word occurs once in all of Scripture; the King James translators kept the Hebrew plural rather than inventing an English form.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 2:19

And when thou comest nigh over against the children of Ammon, distress them not, nor meddle with them: for I will not give thee of the land of the children of Ammon any possession; because I have given it unto the children of Lot for a possession.
Deuteronomy 2:20
(That also was accounted a land of giants: giants dwelt therein in old time; and the Ammonites call them Zamzummims;
Deuteronomy 2:21
A people great, and many, and tall, as the Anakims; but the LORD destroyed them before them; and they succeeded them, and dwelt in their stead:
Genesis 14:5
And in the fourteenth year came Chedorlaomer, and the kings that were with him, and smote the Rephaims in Ashteroth Karnaim, and the Zuzims in Ham, and the Emims in Shaveh Kiriathaim,
Acts 17:26
And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the plain agency of Deuteronomy 2:21 — the LORD destroyed them, and Ammon succeeded them. Nations receive their ground; they do not win it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What wants recovering is the sentence structure of Deuteronomy 2:21, which the modern ear will not hear as written. The LORD destroyed them before them; and they succeeded them, and dwelt in their stead. Ammon is the beneficiary, not the author. God is the only actor with a verb of destruction in the clause. The secular account of the ancient Near East can describe the same events entirely in terms of migration and military capacity, and it will not be wrong about a single fact while being wrong about the whole. Scripture insists that the bounds of habitation are appointed, and it insists on it about a pagan nation to whom no covenant was ever given.

There is a second point, more uncomfortable. God did this for Ammon — a people descended from incest, who would worship Molech, who would thrust out the right eyes of Jabeshgilead, and whom the law would bar from the assembly. Common grace is not a reward. God gives lands, harvests, and victories to nations that will use them badly, and the Christian who expects providence to distribute goods according to merit has not read Deuteronomy 2. The same chapter that forbids Israel to covet Ammon’s land explains that God secured it for them. That is providence, and it is not sentimental.
roots_summary: Hebrew Zamzummim (H2157), from a root meaning to murmur or hum; identified with the Zuzim (H2104) of Genesis 14:5 and reckoned with the Rephaim.
roots_lines: Hebrew Zamzummim (H2157) — Zamzummims; a hapax legomenon, occurring only at Deuteronomy 2:20.
Hebrew Zuzim (H2104) — the Zuzims of Genesis 14:5, generally taken as the same people under another name.
Hebrew Rephaim (H7497) — giants; the class to which Deuteronomy 2:20 assigns them.
Hebrew shamad (H8045) — to destroy, to exterminate; the LORD destroyed them before them (Deuteronomy 2:21).
Hebrew yarash (H3423) — to succeed to, to dispossess; the verb for Ammon’s taking of the land.
usage: The Ammonites call them Zamzummims (Deuteronomy 2:20) — a people named by their neighbours and known by nothing else.
But the LORD destroyed them before them (Deuteronomy 2:21) — the agency Scripture will not let a reader misplace.
The Zuzims in Ham (Genesis 14:5) — the same stock under the older name.

etymology: Hebrew Kaphtorim, the people of Caphtor, listed in the table of nations among the sons of Mizraim (Genesis 10:14). Caphtor is most often identified with Crete and the neighbouring coasts. From this stock came the Philistines, which makes the Caphtorim the ancestors of Israel’s most persistent enemy.
biblical_def: The Caphtorims are a sea people out of the table of nations who crossed to the coast of Canaan and took it. Deuteronomy records the conquest in one clause: the Caphtorims, which came forth out of Caphtor, destroyed them, and dwelt in their stead (Deuteronomy 2:23) — the Avims being the people they displaced from Hazerim to Gaza. From this migration came the Philistines, and both prophets who mention Caphtor say so. Amos puts it in the mouth of the LORD in a sentence that dismantles Israel’s pride: Have not I brought up Israel out of the land of Egypt? and the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Syrians from Kir? (Amos 9:7). Jeremiah, pronouncing the burden of the Philistines, calls them the remnant of the country of Caphtor (Jeremiah 47:4). The doctrine embedded in Amos 9:7 is severe and easy to miss. Israel was inclined to treat the Exodus as proof of her indispensability. God answers by placing it beside two migrations nobody had thought to call redemptive, and by saying that He conducted those as well. The exodus was not less than Israel supposed; her uniqueness was. The God who fetched Israel out of Egypt also fetched the Philistines out of Caphtor, and He would judge her as He judged them.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 carries no CAPHTORIM entry. The name occurs in Genesis 10:14 and 1 Chronicles 1:12 in the table of nations, and in Deuteronomy 2:23; Caphtor itself appears in Jeremiah 47:4 and Amos 9:7.
webster_full: CAPHTORIMS, n. pl. — The people of Caphtor, a maritime country generally identified with Crete; the stock from which the Philistines came.
Genesis 10:14 lists them among the sons of Mizraim, with the Casluhim, out of whom came Philistim.
The King James Version also spells the singular form Caphthorim (1 Chronicles 1:12).
Jeremiah 47:4 and Amos 9:7 both tie Caphtor to the Philistines explicitly.
Webster 1828 does not treat the word; the identification with Crete rests on the geography and on the Cherethites of 1 Samuel 30:14 and Zephaniah 2:5.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 2:23
And the Avims which dwelt in Hazerim, even unto Azzah, the Caphtorims, which came forth out of Caphtor, destroyed them, and dwelt in their stead.)
Amos 9:7

Are ye not as children of the Ethiopians unto me, O children of Israel? saith the LORD. Have not I brought up Israel out of the land of Egypt? and the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Syrians from Kir?
Jeremiah 47:4

Because of the day that cometh to spoil all the Philistines, and to cut off from Tyrus and Zidon every helper that remaineth: for the LORD will spoil the Philistines, the remnant of the country of Caphtor.
Joshua 13:3

From Sihor, which is before Egypt, even unto the borders of Ekron northward, which is counted to the Canaanite: five lords of the Philistines; the Gazathites, and the Ashdothites, the Eshkalonites, the Gittites, and the Ekronites; also the Avites:
Acts 17:26
And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;
corruption_summary: Amos 9:7 is quoted as though it flattened the difference between Israel and the nations into a general divine impartiality. It does the opposite: it removes Israel’s ground of boasting while leaving her election, and her accountability, exactly where they were.
corruption_paragraphs: The progressive use of Amos 9:7 makes it a proof text for religious pluralism — if God brought the Philistines from Caphtor as He brought Israel from Egypt, then no people and no faith is privileged. That reading cannot survive the book it stands in. Amos 3:2 has already said, You only have I known of all the families of the earth: therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities. The two verses are the same argument. Election is real, and it is precisely what makes Israel’s judgment heavier rather than lighter. What Amos 9:7 destroys is not election but presumption: the assumption that having been redeemed once, Israel could sin with impunity. The doctrine is the same one Paul presses on the church — be not highminded, but fear.

The second thing to see is God’s government of migrations that no one at the time called providential. A sea people crossed from Caphtor, drove out the Avim, and settled five cities; four hundred years later their descendants held the ark of God and cut off Saul’s head. Every stage of that had a natural explanation, and every stage was directed. Christians who can see the hand of God in the pleasant turns of their own history and not in the hostile ones have only half the doctrine. The Philistines were brought up from Caphtor by the LORD, and He used them for four centuries as the rod of His discipline.
roots_summary: Hebrew Kaphtorim (H3732), the people of Kaphtor (H3731); associated with the Kerethim (H3774), the Cherethites, and with the Philistines throughout.
roots_lines: Hebrew Kaphtor (H3731) — Caphtor; a maritime land, most commonly identified with Crete.
Hebrew Kaphtorim (H3732) — the Caphtorims; Genesis 10:14, Deuteronomy 2:23, 1 Chronicles 1:12.
Hebrew Pelishtim (H6430) — the Philistines; Genesis 10:14 traces them to this same branch of Mizraim.
Hebrew Kerethim (H3774) — the Cherethites, parallel to the Philistines in 1 Samuel 30:14 and Zephaniah 2:5, and a support for the Cretan identification.
Hebrew she’erith (H7611) — remnant; the remnant of the country of Caphtor (Jeremiah 47:4).
usage: Which came forth out of Caphtor, destroyed them, and dwelt in their stead (Deuteronomy 2:23) — a migration recorded as a conquest.
The Philistines from Caphtor, and the Syrians from Kir (Amos 9:7) — God governs the movements of nations that never knew Him.
The remnant of the country of Caphtor (Jeremiah 47:4) — the Philistines named by their origin at the moment of their end.

etymology: Also Hagarenes in Psalm 83:6; from Hagar, Sarah’s Egyptian handmaid and Ishmael’s mother. A nomadic confederacy of the eastern desert beyond Gilead, they are one of the tribes Scripture reckons as Abraham’s seed after the flesh and outside the covenant.
biblical_def: The Hagarites ranged the desert east of Gilead, and the Chronicler records the war Reuben, Gad, and the half tribe of Manasseh waged against them. The account is short and it is one of the most instructive battle reports in Scripture: they were helped against them, and the Hagarites were delivered into their hand, and all that were with them: for they cried to God in the battle, and he was intreated of them; because they put their trust in him (1 Chronicles 5:20). The next verse adds, because the war was of God. Two and a half tribes who were themselves living east of Jordan by a compromised choice nevertheless prayed in the field and were answered, and the historian will not let the reader attribute the victory to the fifty thousand men who fought it. The Hagarites appear again in Asaph’s psalm among the confederacy plotting against Israel: the tabernacles of Edom, and the Ishmaelites; of Moab, and the Hagarenes (Psalm 83:6). Their name keeps Hagar before us, and Paul makes her an allegory in Galatians 4 — the bondwoman and the free, the son after the flesh and the son by promise. The Hagarites are the flesh’s descendants ranged in arms against the children of promise, which is exactly Paul’s point about the two covenants.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 has no HAGARITE entry. The Authorized Version uses Hagarites in 1 Chronicles 5 and Hagarenes in Psalm 83:6; both render the same Hebrew, and the name looks back to Hagar the Egyptian.
webster_full: HAGARITES, HAGARENES, n. pl. — An Arab people of the desert east of Gilead, reckoned as descendants of Hagar.
The two English forms in the Authorized Version render one Hebrew word; the variation is the translators’.
1 Chronicles 5:19 names their allies: Jetur, Nephish, and Nodab — two of the three being sons of Ishmael (Genesis 25:15).
1 Chronicles 27:31 has Jaziz the Hagerite over David’s flocks, so the people were not uniformly hostile.
Webster 1828 does not carry the term; the biblical usage is confined to Chronicles and Psalm 83.
scriptures: 1 Chronicles 5:10
And in the days of Saul they made war with the Hagarites, who fell by their hand: and they dwelt in their tents throughout all the east land of Gilead.
1 Chronicles 5:20

And they were helped against them, and the Hagarites were delivered into their hand, and all that were with them: for they cried to God in the battle, and he was intreated of them; because they put their trust in him.
1 Chronicles 5:22
For there fell down many slain, because the war was of God. And they dwelt in their steads until the captivity.
Psalm 83:6
The tabernacles of Edom, and the Ishmaelites; of Moab, and the Hagarenes;
Genesis 16:12
And he will be a wild man; his hand will be against every man, and every man’s hand against him; and he shall dwell in the presence of all his brethren.
corruption_summary: 1 Chronicles 5:20 is a favourite text of the prosperity teachers, who read it as a formula: trust, and the enemy is delivered. The same chapter ends with these tribes carried away by Assyria for the sin the Chronicler names, which is what a formula cannot survive.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse is genuinely a promise-shaped verse — they cried to God in the battle, and he was intreated of them; because they put their trust in him — and it deserves to be preached as one. What must not be done is to lift it out of its chapter. Twenty-six verses later the same tribes are described as transgressing against the God of their fathers and going a whoring after the gods of the people of the land, and God stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria and carried them away. The Chronicler has deliberately set the answered prayer and the captivity in one paragraph. A cry in extremity is heard; it does not purchase a covenant of exemption. Prosperity preaching lives entirely in verse 20 and never reads on to verse 26.

The deeper matter is Hagar herself, and Paul’s use of her in Galatians 4. The bondwoman’s son was born after the flesh, the freewoman’s by promise, and Paul says these are the two covenants. Ishmael was circumcised, was Abraham’s true son, received a real blessing and became a great nation — and was not the heir. That is the sharpest possible statement of the difference between natural descent and sovereign promise, and it is why the Hagarites belong in a Reformed dictionary. Every religion of human effort is Hagar’s child: sincere, energetic, genuinely fruitful in its way, and not the seed to whom the inheritance was given.
roots_summary: Hebrew Hagri (H1905), Hagarite, from Hagar (H1904); the confederacy of 1 Chronicles 5:19 is joined with Ishmael’s sons Jetur and Nephish.
roots_lines: Hebrew Hagar (H1904) — Hagar; Sarah’s Egyptian handmaid, Ishmael’s mother (Genesis 16:1).
Hebrew Hagri (H1905) — Hagarite, Hagerite, Hagarene; the desert people reckoned from her.
Hebrew Yetur (H3195) and Naphish (H5305) — Jetur and Nephish, sons of Ishmael (Genesis 25:15) and allies of the Hagarites.
Hebrew atar (H6279) — to entreat, to be prevailed upon by entreaty; he was intreated of them (1 Chronicles 5:20).
Greek Agar (G28) — Hagar; Paul’s allegory of the two covenants in Galatians 4:24-25.
usage: They cried to God in the battle, and he was intreated of them (1 Chronicles 5:20) — prayer in the field, answered.
Because the war was of God (1 Chronicles 5:22) — the Chronicler’s refusal to credit the fifty thousand.
Of Moab, and the Hagarenes (Psalm 83:6) — the flesh’s children confederate against the church.

etymology: Also spelled Ishmeelites in the Authorized Version’s Genesis narratives; from Ishmael, Abraham’s son by Hagar. Twelve princes according to their nations (Genesis 25:16), they became the caravan peoples of the northern Arabian desert, known by their camels, their spice trade, and their golden earrings.
biblical_def: The Ishmaelites are Abraham’s seed by the bondwoman, and their first appearance in Scripture is one of the great turning points of providence. Judah looked up from the pit and saw a company of Ishmeelites… with their camels bearing spicery and balm and myrrh, going to carry it down to Egypt (Genesis 37:25), and proposed the sale that put Joseph on the road to Potiphar’s house, the prison, and the throne. The narrative calls the same traders Midianites in one verse and Ishmeelites in the next, both peoples being Abraham’s children by other mothers and both riding the same desert routes. Gideon’s spoil is explained by an aside on their custom: they had golden earrings, because they were Ishmaelites (Judges 8:24). Asaph lists them among the nations confederate against the people of God (Psalm 83:6). The angel’s word to Hagar frames the whole history: he will be a wild man; his hand will be against every man, and every man’s hand against him (Genesis 16:12). And yet God heard the boy crying in the wilderness of Beersheba, gave him a nation and twelve princes, and kept every syllable of what He promised Abraham about him. Ishmael is proof that God’s temporal kindness and His covenant election are not the same gift.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 has no ISHMAELITE entry in the biblical sense, though the English word had already begun its proverbial use for an outcast or one at war with society, drawn straight from Genesis 16:12.
webster_full: ISHMAELITE, n. — A descendant of Ishmael, the son of Abraham by Hagar; one of the Arab peoples of the northern desert.
The Authorized Version prints Ishmeelites in Genesis 37 and 39, Ishmaelites in Judges 8 and Psalm 83; the Hebrew is one word.
Genesis 25:13-16 names his twelve sons, twelve princes according to their nations, fulfilling Genesis 17:20.
The proverbial English sense — an Ishmael, a man whose hand is against every man — comes directly from the angel’s words in Genesis 16:12.
Webster 1828 does not carry the biblical gentilic; the sense is fixed by Genesis, Judges, and the Psalms.
scriptures: Genesis 16:12
And he will be a wild man; his hand will be against every man, and every man’s hand against him; and he shall dwell in the presence of all his brethren.
Genesis 37:25

And they sat down to eat bread: and they lifted up their eyes and looked, and, behold, a company of Ishmeelites came from Gilead with their camels bearing spicery and balm and myrrh, going to carry it down to Egypt.
Genesis 37:27
Come, and let us sell him to the Ishmeelites, and let not our hand be upon him; for he is our brother and our flesh. And his brethren were content.
Judges 8:24
And Gideon said unto them, I would desire a request of you, that ye would give me every man the earrings of his prey. (For they had golden earrings, because they were Ishmaelites.)
Psalm 83:6
The tabernacles of Edom, and the Ishmaelites; of Moab, and the Hagarenes;
corruption_summary: Ishmael is the standing counter-example to the assumption that God’s outward blessing marks His covenant favour. Twelve princes, a great nation, and a heard prayer — and the covenant went to the other son.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul builds the doctrine of election on exactly this pair in Romans 9 and Galatians 4, and the modern instinct is to soften it into a lesson about God’s care for outsiders. His care for Ishmael is real and Scripture insists on it: God heard the lad, opened Hagar’s eyes to the well, was with him as he grew, and made of him a nation. But the covenant was established with Isaac, and God said so before Isaac was born. This is the point at which every scheme of salvation by natural descent, by sincerity, or by religious effort breaks. Ishmael had Abraham’s blood, Abraham’s household, Abraham’s circumcision, and Abraham’s prayer offered for him by name — O that Ishmael might live before thee! — and the inheritance still passed by promise, not by flesh.

The second corruption is a sentimentality that will not look at Genesis 37. A caravan of Abraham’s own descendants bought Abraham’s great-grandson for twenty pieces of silver and carried him into slavery, and Joseph afterward told his brethren, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good. The Ishmaelite traders were not innocent, the brothers were not innocent, and God was not thereby made the author of their sin. He governed it. That is the Reformed doctrine of concurrence stated in a narrative rather than a proposition, and it is the only doctrine that can look at a real evil and still say that the throne was never empty.
roots_summary: Hebrew Yishma’el (H3458), God shall hear, from shama to hear and El, God; the gentilic is Yishme’eli (H3459).
roots_lines: Hebrew Yishma’el (H3458) — Ishmael, God shall hear; named at Genesis 16:11 because the LORD hath heard thy affliction.
Hebrew Yishme’eli (H3459) — Ishmeelite, Ishmaelite; the gentilic of Genesis 37 and Judges 8.
Hebrew pere adam — a wild man, literally a wild ass of a man (Genesis 16:12), figuring a free and untamed desert life.
Hebrew nesi’im — princes; twelve princes according to their nations (Genesis 25:16), answering the promise of Genesis 17:20.
Greek Ismael — not named in the Greek New Testament, though Galatians 4:22-31 argues the whole history without using the name.
usage: His hand will be against every man (Genesis 16:12) — the angel’s summary of a nation’s temper.
A company of Ishmeelites… going to carry it down to Egypt (Genesis 37:25) — the caravan providence used.
Because they were Ishmaelites (Judges 8:24) — the golden earrings that became Gideon’s ephod and Israel’s snare.

etymology: Hebrew Qenizzi, from Kenaz, a duke of Edom (Genesis 36:11, 15). The Authorized Version also renders the adjective Kenezite, the title given to Caleb the son of Jephunneh — a man of Edomite descent who becomes the boldest believer of his generation in Israel.
biblical_def: The Kenizzites are named once in the land grant to Abraham, in the list of ten peoples whose country was promised to his seed: The Kenites, and the Kenizzites, and the Kadmonites (Genesis 15:19). The name derives from Kenaz, a duke in the line of Esau, and this is what gives the word its remarkable second use. Caleb, who with Joshua alone brought back a good report from the spies and who alone with Joshua entered the land of his generation, is four times called the son of Jephunneh the Kenezite. The LORD’s own commendation is attached to the title: Save Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenezite, and Joshua the son of Nun: for they have wholly followed the LORD (Numbers 32:12). And when the inheritance is finally given, the narrator keeps the title: Hebron therefore became the inheritance of Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenezite unto this day, because that he wholly followed the LORD God of Israel (Joshua 14:14). Hebron is the city of Abraham’s grave and the stronghold of the Anakim, and it goes to a man whose lineage traces to Esau, reckoned into Judah, who asked at eighty-five for the mountain with the giants on it. The peoples of Genesis 15:19 were to be dispossessed; one of their sons received the choicest portion of the land by faith.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 has no KENIZZITE entry. The gentilic occurs once (Genesis 15:19); the personal epithet Kenezite occurs of Caleb and of Othniel’s father Kenaz, and the tie between the two is genealogical.
webster_full: KENIZZITES, n. pl. — A people of the south country named in the promise to Abraham (Genesis 15:19); reckoned from Kenaz.
KENEZITE, n. — The epithet of Caleb the son of Jephunneh (Numbers 32:12; Joshua 14:6, 14).
Kenaz was a duke of Edom, grandson of Esau (Genesis 36:11, 15), and a Kenaz also stands as father of Othniel, Israel’s first judge (Judges 3:9).
Caleb is nevertheless numbered with the tribe of Judah (Numbers 13:6), the household having been reckoned into Israel.
Webster 1828 does not treat the word; the sense is wholly biblical and genealogical.
scriptures: Genesis 15:19
The Kenites, and the Kenizzites, and the Kadmonites,
Numbers 32:12
Save Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenezite, and Joshua the son of Nun: for they have wholly followed the LORD.
Joshua 14:14
Hebron therefore became the inheritance of Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenezite unto this day, because that he wholly followed the LORD God of Israel.
Deuteronomy 23:7
Thou shalt not abhor an Edomite; for he is thy brother: thou shalt not abhor an Egyptian; because thou wast a stranger in his land.
Acts 17:26
And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that faith, not pedigree, is what Scripture praises, and that God grafts in whom He pleases without loosening a single requirement of obedience.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The recovery is a doctrine hidden in a genealogical footnote. Caleb is named a Kenezite four times, and the phrase he wholly followed the LORD is attached to him six times in the Pentateuch and Joshua. Scripture does not treat the two facts as being in tension; it puts them side by side, and never suggests that Caleb’s descent needed explaining away. He asked for Hebron because the sons of Anak were there. The men of pure descent had refused that mountain forty years earlier and died in the wilderness for it. Faith is not the property of a bloodline, which is the whole burden of Hebrews 11 and the reason Rahab and Ruth stand in it.

The corollary needs saying plainly, because the doctrine is often stated half-way. Caleb was not received into Israel while remaining outside her worship, her law, or her covenant. He is numbered with Judah, he keeps the LORD’s commandments, and his confession is that the LORD will bring the people into the land. Grafting in is real, and it is total. The modern demand that the church receive people on their own terms and celebrate what they bring with them has nothing in common with Caleb, who brought nothing but a whole heart and asked for a mountain full of giants.
roots_summary: Hebrew Qenizzi (H7074), Kenizzite or Kenezite, from Qenaz (H7073), Kenaz, a duke of Edom; the same form serves the people and Caleb’s epithet.
roots_lines: Hebrew Qenaz (H7073) — Kenaz; son of Eliphaz and duke of Edom (Genesis 36:11, 15), and the father of Othniel (Judges 3:9).
Hebrew Qenizzi (H7074) — Kenizzite, Kenezite; Genesis 15:19 of the people, Numbers 32:12 of Caleb.
Hebrew male achar YHWH — to fill up after the LORD, the idiom the King James renders wholly followed the LORD (Numbers 32:12).
Hebrew Kaleb (H3612) — Caleb; the name is connected with the word for dog, and he asked for the hardest ground in Canaan.
Hebrew Chebron (H2275) — Hebron; Abraham’s burial place and the Anakim stronghold given to Caleb.
usage: The Kenites, and the Kenizzites, and the Kadmonites (Genesis 15:19) — the peoples named in Abraham’s land grant.
Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenezite… wholly followed the LORD (Numbers 32:12) — descent and commendation in one sentence.
Hebron therefore became the inheritance of Caleb (Joshua 14:14) — the giants’ mountain given to the man who asked for it.

etymology: From Jerahmeel, meaning may God have compassion, the firstborn of Hezron of the tribe of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:9, 25). Their cities lay in the dry south country of Judah, the Negeb, where David sheltered during his exile among the Philistines.
biblical_def: The Jerahmeelites are a clan of Judah, descended from Hezron’s firstborn, whose settlements lay in the south country toward the wilderness. They appear only in the David narratives, and both appearances are worth weighing together. In the first, David is a fugitive living at Ziklag under Achish of Gath, raiding the Geshurites and Amalekites and killing every witness, and when the Philistine king asks where he has been, David lies: Against the south of Judah, and against the south of the Jerahmeelites, and against the south of the Kenites (1 Samuel 27:10). He names his own kinsmen as the people he has been plundering, precisely so that Achish will think him hated in Israel. In the second, David has recovered the spoil of Ziklag from the Amalekites, and he sends portions of it to the elders of Judah — and to them which were in the cities of the Jerahmeelites, and to them which were in the cities of the Kenites (1 Samuel 30:29). The same clan he had slandered receives his gift. Scripture gives the deceit and the restitution without comment, three chapters apart, and lets the reader see a man of God at his worst and then at his most generous, in the same wilderness, toward the same people.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 has no JERAHMEELITE entry. The name is Hebrew, may God have compassion, and the clan is confined to 1 Samuel 27 and 30 and the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 2.
webster_full: JERAHMEELITES, n. pl. — A family of the tribe of Judah descended from Jerahmeel the son of Hezron, dwelling in the south of Judah.
The name is composed of the Hebrew for to have compassion and El, God: God will have compassion.
1 Chronicles 2:9 and 2:25-41 preserve the genealogy at unusual length for so obscure a house.
Their territory is the Negeb, the dry south country toward Beersheba and the wilderness of Judah.
Webster 1828 does not treat the word; the two narratives in 1 Samuel supply its whole biblical use.
scriptures: 1 Chronicles 2:9
The sons also of Hezron, that were born unto him; Jerahmeel, and Ram, and Chelubai.
1 Chronicles 2:25
And the sons of Jerahmeel the firstborn of Hezron were, Ram the firstborn, and Bunah, and Oren, and Ozem, and Ahijah.
1 Samuel 27:10
And Achish said, Whither have ye made a road to day? And David said, Against the south of Judah, and against the south of the Jerahmeelites, and against the south of the Kenites.
1 Samuel 30:29
And to them which were in Rachal, and to them which were in the cities of the Jerahmeelites, and to them which were in the cities of the Kenites,
Psalm 32:5
I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid. I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the LORD; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin. Selah.
corruption_summary: The Ziklag chapters are regularly cleaned up in retellings of David’s life. Scripture does not clean them up, and the honesty of the record is one of the strongest evidences that the histories are not hagiography.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Samuel 27 is an uncomfortable chapter. David says in his heart that he shall now perish by the hand of Saul, which is unbelief spoken plainly after years of promises; he takes refuge with the Philistine king he had once fled from in feigned madness; he raids and leaves no survivor so that no report can reach Gath; and he lies about it, naming Judah, the Jerahmeelites, and the Kenites as his victims. The Holy Ghost records all of it about the man after God’s own heart. Scripture’s saints are not presented as examples of unbroken integrity, and any biography of David that smooths this over has traded the doctrine of remaining sin for a moral tale. The Reformed reading is the honest one: David is justified by an imputed righteousness and not by his conduct at Ziklag.

The second half of the account is the gospel’s shape in miniature. Three chapters later David, having recovered everything the Amalekites took, sends spoil to the elders of Judah and to the cities of the Jerahmeelites and the Kenites — the very names he had used to cover his tracks. He also rules, against the sons of Belial in his own company, that the man who tarries by the stuff shares alike with the man who goes down to the battle. A man freshly given more than he lost becomes generous toward those he had wronged. That is repentance in its ordinary clothing, and it is far more convincing than a David who never lied.
roots_summary: Hebrew Yerachme’el (H3396), God will have compassion, from racham to have mercy and El, God; the gentilic is Yerachme’eli (H3397).
roots_lines: Hebrew Yerachme’el (H3396) — Jerahmeel; may God have compassion.
Hebrew racham (H7355) — to love deeply, to have compassion; the root of the tender-mercies vocabulary of the Psalms.
Hebrew Yerachme’eli (H3397) — Jerahmeelite; 1 Samuel 27:10 and 30:29 only.
Hebrew Chetsron (H2696) — Hezron; son of Pharez, in the line from Judah to David (Ruth 4:18-19).
Hebrew negeb (H5045) — the south, the dry country; the region the Authorized Version renders the south in 1 Samuel 27:10.
usage: Against the south of the Jerahmeelites (1 Samuel 27:10) — the lie David told Achish about his own kinsmen.
To them which were in the cities of the Jerahmeelites (1 Samuel 30:29) — the same clan receiving his spoil.
The sons also of Hezron… Jerahmeel, and Ram (1 Chronicles 2:9) — a house of Judah kept in the record.

etymology: Hebrew Maon, a habitation or dwelling; the Maonites are an Arabian people of the south, almost certainly the Mehunims of Chronicles. The same Hebrew word is used of God Himself as the dwelling place of His people, which gives the name an ironic edge.
biblical_def: The Maonites appear once by that name, in the LORD’s own recital of Israel’s deliverances when she came again to Him in the days of Jephthah: The Zidonians also, and the Amalekites, and the Maonites, did oppress you; and ye cried to me, and I delivered you out of their hand (Judges 10:12). They are almost certainly the Mehunims whom Uzziah subdued — God helped him against the Philistines, and against the Arabians that dwelt in Gurbaal, and the Mehunims (2 Chronicles 26:7) — and whom the Ammonites brought against Jehoshaphat. Their importance lies entirely in the sentence they stand in. Judges 10 is the LORD’s answer to a people who had served Baalim and Ashtaroth and the gods of Syria, Zidon, Moab, Ammon, and the Philistines, and who now cried for deliverance. He lists seven oppressors He had already saved them from, and then says, Go and cry unto the gods which ye have chosen; let them deliver you in the time of your tribulation. The Maonites are one item in a divine indictment. And when Israel put away the strange gods and served the LORD, the record adds that his soul was grieved for the misery of Israel. That is the God the Maonites were used to discipline, and the God who could not finally be provoked out of pity.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 has no MAONITE entry. The Hebrew maon means a dwelling or habitation, and is the word used in Psalm 90:1 and Deuteronomy 33:27 for God as the refuge of His people.
webster_full: MAONITES, n. pl. — An Arabian people south of Judah who oppressed Israel in the days of the judges; probably the Mehunims of 2 Chronicles.
The Hebrew root maon signifies a dwelling, a habitation, a den.
The same word describes God in Psalm 90:1, Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations.
2 Chronicles 20:1 and 26:7 mention the Mehunims among the confederacies against Judah, and the identification with the Maonites is the usual one.
There is also a Maon in the hill country of Judah, David’s hiding place and Nabal’s district (1 Samuel 23:24-25; 25:2), a distinct place of the same name.
scriptures: Judges 10:12
The Zidonians also, and the Amalekites, and the Maonites, did oppress you; and ye cried to me, and I delivered you out of their hand.
2 Chronicles 26:7
And God helped him against the Philistines, and against the Arabians that dwelt in Gurbaal, and the Mehunims.
Judges 10:14
Go and cry unto the gods which ye have chosen; let them deliver you in the time of your tribulation.
Judges 10:16
And they put away the strange gods from among them, and served the LORD: and his soul was grieved for the misery of Israel.
Psalm 90:1
Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations.
corruption_summary: Judges 10:14 is one of the sharpest sentences God ever spoke to His own people, and it is almost never preached. A God who cannot say go and cry unto the gods which ye have chosen is not the God of Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic account of God cannot accommodate Judges 10:14. Israel cries in distress and God tells her to take the complaint to the gods she preferred. That is holy irony, and it is meant to wound. It is also the necessary preface to what follows: only after that word do they put away the strange gods, and only then does the text say that his soul was grieved for the misery of Israel. Repentance in Scripture is not produced by reassurance. It is produced by God refusing to be one option among the gods a man has chosen, and the refusal is itself an act of mercy. Any preaching that skips verse 14 to reach verse 16 has removed the instrument God used.

The second thing to notice is the impassibility question the King James phrase raises. His soul was grieved is an anthropopathism — Scripture’s way of speaking of God after the manner of men, so that creatures can understand what is unchangeably true of Him. The Reformed confession holds God to be without body, parts, or passions, and holds at the same time that the compassion here declared is real and not a fiction. God is not moved from outside as we are moved; His mercy is His own eternal nature turned toward His people in time. Open theism reads such verses as evidence that God changes His mind and learns; the classical doctrine reads them as God stooping to speak in our language about what He has always been.
roots_summary: Hebrew Meunim or Maon (H4584), from maon (H4583), a dwelling or habitation; the same noun is used of God as His people’s dwelling place.
roots_lines: Hebrew maon (H4583) — a dwelling, habitation, den; Psalm 90:1 of God Himself.
Hebrew Meunim (H4586) — Mehunims; the people of 2 Chronicles 26:7 generally identified with the Maonites.
Hebrew lachats (H3905) — to press, to oppress; the verb of Judges 10:12.
Hebrew qatsar (H7114) — to be short, to be shortened; the idiom behind his soul was grieved (Judges 10:16) is that God’s soul was shortened for Israel’s misery.
The Maon of 1 Samuel 23-25, in the hill country of Judah, is a separate location bearing the same common noun.
usage: The Zidonians also, and the Amalekites, and the Maonites, did oppress you (Judges 10:12) — one name in a list of seven deliverances.
Go and cry unto the gods which ye have chosen (Judges 10:14) — the sentence that produced Israel’s repentance.
Against the Arabians that dwelt in Gurbaal, and the Mehunims (2 Chronicles 26:7) — the same people under the Chronicler’s name.

etymology: Inhabitants of Gath, one of the five Philistine cities; Hebrew Gitti. Gath means a winepress. The word covers Goliath, the six hundred men who followed David out of Jerusalem, and Obededom in whose house the ark rested three months and was blessed.
biblical_def: The Gittites are men of Gath, and Scripture uses them to show that no nation is beyond the reach of grace. Gath produced Goliath, whose brother… the Gittite Elhanan afterward slew (2 Samuel 21:19). Gath sheltered David twice in his exile. And Gath supplied two of the most striking figures in the David narrative. When the ark struck Uzzah and David feared to bring it further, he turned it aside into the house of Obededom the Gittite, and it remained there three months, and the LORD blessed Obededom, and all his household (2 Samuel 6:11) — the ark that killed an Israelite for irreverence blessing a Philistine household for reverence. Then, on the day David fled from Absalom, six hundred Gittites marched with him, and the king tried to send their captain home: Wherefore goest thou also with us? return to thy place, and abide with the king: for thou art a stranger, and also an exile (2 Samuel 15:19). Ittai’s answer is one of the great confessions of loyalty in Scripture: as the LORD liveth, and as my lord the king liveth, surely in what place my lord the king shall be, whether in death or life, even there also will thy servant be. A Philistine, newly come, chose the rejected king when Israel’s own men chose Absalom.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 has no GITTITE entry. Gath is Hebrew for a winepress, and the gentilic denotes its inhabitants; the Authorized Version also uses Gittith in three psalm titles, probably an instrument or tune of Gath.
webster_full: GITTITE, n. — An inhabitant of Gath, one of the five lordships of the Philistines.
Hebrew gath signifies a winepress, a common element in Palestinian place names (Gathhepher, Gathrimmon).
The psalm titles of Psalms 8, 81, and 84 read upon Gittith, generally taken as an instrument or melody associated with Gath.
Six hundred Gittites followed David from Gath and formed part of his guard alongside the Cherethites and Pelethites (2 Samuel 15:18).
Webster 1828 does not carry the word; the sense comes from Joshua 13:3 and the books of Samuel.
scriptures: Joshua 13:3

From Sihor, which is before Egypt, even unto the borders of Ekron northward, which is counted to the Canaanite: five lords of the Philistines; the Gazathites, and the Ashdothites, the Eshkalonites, the Gittites, and the Ekronites; also the Avites:
2 Samuel 6:11
And the ark of the LORD continued in the house of Obededom the Gittite three months: and the LORD blessed Obededom, and all his household.
2 Samuel 15:19
Then said the king to Ittai the Gittite, Wherefore goest thou also with us? return to thy place, and abide with the king: for thou art a stranger, and also an exile.
2 Samuel 15:21

And Ittai answered the king, and said, As the LORD liveth, and as my lord the king liveth, surely in what place my lord the king shall be, whether in death or life, even there also will thy servant be.
2 Samuel 15:22
And David said to Ittai, Go and pass over. And Ittai the Gittite passed over, and all his men, and all the little ones that were with him.
corruption_summary: Ittai’s oath is the plainest picture in the Old Testament of what it costs to follow a rejected king, and it is the exact opposite of the modern gospel invitation that promises the believer the winning side.
corruption_paragraphs: David offered Ittai every reason to leave: he was a stranger, an exile, newly come, and the throne was going the other way. Ittai swore by the LORD and by the king that he would be wherever the king was, in death or life, and took his men and his little ones over the brook Kidron with him. Our Lord crossed that same brook on the night He was betrayed, and He had already told the multitudes to count the cost, to hate father and mother in comparison, and to take up the cross. A church that recruits by promising cultural respectability and personal flourishing is not preaching the terms David laid before Ittai, nor the terms Christ laid before the crowd. The convert who understands the offer is the one who says whether in death or life.

The Obededom narrative teaches the complementary point. The ark had just killed Uzzah for steadying it with his hand, and David was afraid of it. Into a Gittite’s house it went, and for three months that household was blessed — so plainly that the report of it drew David back to fetch the ark properly, with Levites bearing it as the law prescribed. The same presence of God is death to presumption and blessing to reverence, and the difference is not nationality. It never was. To this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word.
roots_summary: Hebrew Gath (H1661), a winepress; Gitti (H1663), Gittite; the Gittith (H1665) of three psalm titles is probably an instrument or tune of Gath.
roots_lines: Hebrew gath (H1660) — a winepress; the common noun behind the city name.
Hebrew Gath (H1661) — Gath; one of the five Philistine lordships, Goliath’s city.
Hebrew Gitti (H1663) — Gittite; used of Obededom, of Ittai, and of Goliath’s brother.
Hebrew Gittith (H1665) — the superscription of Psalms 8, 81, and 84, upon Gittith.
Hebrew Obed Edom (H5654) — Obededom, servant of Edom; his house was blessed while the ark lodged there (2 Samuel 6:11).
usage: The LORD blessed Obededom, and all his household (2 Samuel 6:11) — the ark that slew Uzzah blessing a Gittite’s house.
Thou art a stranger, and also an exile (2 Samuel 15:19) — every reason Ittai had to go home.
Whether in death or life, even there also will thy servant be (2 Samuel 15:21) — the answer of a Philistine to a fleeing king.

etymology: The Authorized Version’s rendering of Hebrew Kush, the land south of Egypt beyond the cataracts, named for Cush the son of Ham (Genesis 10:6). Webster 1828 defines ETHIOPIAN as a native of Ethiopia, a negro, and the English proverb about changing one’s skin comes directly from Jeremiah 13:23.
biblical_def: The Ethiopians are the people of Cush, the land beyond the rivers south of Egypt, and Scripture gives them a fuller and more honourable place than most readers expect. Moses married an Ethiopian woman, and when Miriam and Aaron spoke against him for it, the LORD did not rebuke the marriage but struck Miriam leprous for the murmuring (Numbers 12:1). Zerah the Ethiopian came against Asa with a host of a thousand thousand, and Asa prayed the great prayer of the weak — LORD, it is nothing with thee to help, whether with many, or with them that have no power — and the LORD smote the Ethiopians before Asa (2 Chronicles 14:12). Jeremiah’s proverb, Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots?, is Scripture’s sharpest single statement of the doctrine of total depravity: the point is not the skin but the impossibility of self-reformation. And when Jeremiah lay sinking in the dungeon of Malchiah with no Israelite lifting a hand, it was Ebedmelech the Ethiopian eunuch who went to the king and drew him out with old rags under his armholes, and to whom the LORD sent a personal word of deliverance because thou hast put thy trust in me (Jeremiah 39:18). The line runs on into Acts 8, where an Ethiopian eunuch reading Isaiah 53 in a chariot is the first recorded convert carried from Jerusalem toward the ends of the earth.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ETHIOPIAN as a native of Ethiopia, and as an adjective, pertaining to Ethiopia; he also records ETHIOPS as a term in the old chemistry, and the proverbial force of Jeremiah’s question was already fixed in English by his day.
webster_full: ETHIOPIAN, a. — Pertaining to Ethiopia, a country in Africa south of Egypt.
ETHIOPIAN, n. — A native of Ethiopia.
The Hebrew is Cush, from Cush the son of Ham (Genesis 10:6); the Septuagint and the Vulgate render it Ethiopia, and the King James translators followed them.
The proverb can the Ethiopian change his skin (Jeremiah 13:23) had entered ordinary English long before 1828 and is used there of any settled habit.
Candace in Acts 8:27 is a dynastic title of the queens of Meroe rather than a personal name, as Pharaoh is of the kings of Egypt.
scriptures: Numbers 12:1
And Miriam and Aaron spake against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman whom he had married: for he had married an Ethiopian woman.
2 Chronicles 14:12
So the LORD smote the Ethiopians before Asa, and before Judah; and the Ethiopians fled.
Jeremiah 13:23
Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil.
Jeremiah 39:18
For I will surely deliver thee, and thou shalt not fall by the sword, but thy life shall be for a prey unto thee: because thou hast put thy trust in me, saith the LORD.
Psalm 68:31
Princes shall come out of Egypt; Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God.
corruption_summary: Jeremiah 13:23 is regularly mishandled in two opposite directions — pressed into service by racialist readers who make it a verse about skin, and blunted by moralists who make it a verse about difficulty rather than impossibility.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse is a proverb of impossibility, and the prophet says what it means in the same breath: then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil. A man can no more reform his own heart than an Ethiopian can change his complexion or a leopard his coat, and neither the skin nor the spots are presented as defects. They are presented as fixed. This is the doctrine of total depravity stated in a figure — not that man is as bad as he could be, but that the will is bound and cannot originate its own renewal. Jeremiah 31 gives the only remedy: a new covenant, a law written on the heart, a work done by God upon a people who could not do it for themselves. Ezekiel says the same with a heart of stone exchanged for a heart of flesh.

The racialist misuse of the verse, whether by nineteenth-century apologists for slavery or by their modern mirror image, is a straightforward abuse of the text and of the whole canon. Scripture’s Ethiopians are Moses’ wife, whom God defended against Miriam; Ebedmelech, whose trust in the LORD is commended when Zedekiah’s court had none; and the eunuch of Acts 8, baptized on his confession that Jesus Christ is the Son of God. Paul told Athens that God hath made of one blood all nations of men. There is one race in Scripture, the race of Adam, and one dividing line, which is Christ. Any doctrine of blood that adds a second line is a false anthropology, and both the old segregationist reading and the new identitarian one fall under the same condemnation.
roots_summary: Hebrew Kush (H3568), Cush, Ethiopia, from Cush the son of Ham; Kushi (H3569) is the Ethiopian; Greek Aithiops (G128).
roots_lines: Hebrew Kush (H3568) — Cush; the son of Ham (Genesis 10:6) and the land south of Egypt.
Hebrew Kushi (H3569) — Ethiopian, Cushite; used of Moses’ wife, of Zerah, and of Ebedmelech.
Hebrew Ebed Melek (H5663) — Ebedmelech, servant of the king; the eunuch who drew Jeremiah out of the dungeon.
Greek Aithiops (G128) — Ethiopian; Acts 8:27 of the eunuch of Candace.
Greek Kandake (G2582) — Candace; a dynastic title of the queens of Meroe, not a personal name.
usage: Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? (Jeremiah 13:23) — the bondage of the will stated as a proverb.
So the LORD smote the Ethiopians before Asa (2 Chronicles 14:12) — a thousand thousand broken after a prayer.
Because thou hast put thy trust in me (Jeremiah 39:18) — God’s personal word to an Ethiopian eunuch in a doomed city.
